excerpts.text: I hold that a meaningful sentence works by picturing a possible state of affairs, its simple parts standing for simple things. Whatever cannot be pictured so, such as ethics or logical form itself, cannot be said, only shown.
I hold that if good or bad willing changes the world, it can only alter the limits of the world, not the facts, which are the things expressible in language.
I hold that the sentences of everyday language are, just as they stand, in perfect logical order.

I hold that words get their meaning from the many ways they are used in shared activities, not from naming or picturing. Nothing single is common to everything we call language, and meaning is not fixed by hidden logical structure.

I hold that having a mental state just is being in a computational state of a machine-like system: believing or desiring something is fixed entirely by the state's role in the program the organism is running.
I hold that psychological states are not analysable as mere dispositions to behave, so behaviourism leaves out the internal organization that explains behaviour.
I hold that the same kind of mental state can be had by creatures with very different physical makeup, so mental kinds are not identical to specific brain-state kinds.

I hold that what a belief or desire is depends on the surrounding physical and social environment, so no internal computational state can fix it; theories identifying mental states with such states miss their nature.

I hold that the best explanation of why our mature scientific theories work so well is that they are at least approximately true descriptions of a mind-independent world; denying this leaves their success unexplained.
I hold that ordinary speakers rely on experts to fix the reference of terms like the names of tree species, so meaning involves a division of linguistic labour.
I hold that what our words refer to is partly fixed by the surrounding environment, not by what is in the speaker's head.

I hold that no description of the world is available from outside all conceptual schemes; truth is rational acceptability under good conditions within a scheme, and a theory's success does not show it mirrors a ready-made world.

I hold that someone who knew every physical fact about colour vision could still learn something new on first seeing red; so there are non-physical features of experience that no physical story captures.
I hold that we know about other minds partly by inference from behaviour, which is why we think stones do not feel and dogs do.
I hold that what counts as physical information is broad: it includes the functional role of states, along with what the physical, chemical and biological sciences report.

I hold that experience is wholly physical: someone who knew every physical fact would gain no new information on first seeing red, only new abilities, and the sense that something is missing is an illusion.

I hold that a sentence says something factual only if some possible observation would count for or against it; everything else is a tautology of logic and mathematics, or meaningless, and that includes all metaphysics.
I hold that philosophy is a kind of analysis: the philosopher is concerned with the way we speak about things, not with the physical properties of things.
I hold that moral judgements do not state facts; they express feelings of approval or disapproval about actions or situations.

I hold that no precise test of factual meaning has been formulated that is neither too permissive nor too restrictive, and that reducing ordinary statements to reports of sense-experience fails, though the broader suspicion of metaphysics is sound.

I hold that a just society can remain stable because its citizens, sharing one comprehensive moral outlook, come to affirm justice as part of their overall conception of the good.
I hold that moral principles are justified by adjusting general principles and considered judgements against one another until they cohere.

I hold that equal basic liberties for all citizens take priority, and social and economic inequalities are acceptable only if attached to fair opportunity and to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged.

I hold that, since reasonable citizens will always disagree about the whole truth, a just society's stability must rest on a limited set of principles for public life that each person can endorse from within their own, different, worldview.

I hold that only a state limited to protection against force, theft and fraud is justified; taxation for redistribution is wrongful, since people may do what they like with what they justly hold.
I hold that persons are ends in themselves and may not be used merely as means to the ends of others.

I hold that a view confining government to protecting individual rights leaves out humane concerns and joint cooperative activity, and that some further governmental measures, such as antidiscrimination laws, can be legitimate.

I hold that what is good is the satisfaction of preferences, so we should act to maximize the satisfaction of everyone's preferences, weighed equally.
I hold that affluent people are obliged to give to relieve severe poverty abroad when they can do so without sacrificing something of comparable moral importance.
I hold that ethical judgement must be made from a universal point of view, so my own wants cannot count for more than anyone else's simply because they are mine.

I hold that the good consists in certain mental states, pleasure above all, rather than in satisfied desires, since reason can show us goods we have no present desire for; right acts maximize that good impartially.

I hold that the proper starting point is to presume that no God exists, so the burden of proof lies on those who assert one, and the evidence offered so far does not meet it.
I hold that the order of the universe and the origin of life point to an intelligent source, a God of the kind described by deists, though not one who intervenes in history or promises an afterlife.

I hold that numbers, classes, relations and even imaginary things are real entities in a timeless realm, so every meaningful word must stand for some thing, and denying that anything nameable has being is always false.
I hold that mathematics and logic are identical: pure mathematics is the class of all propositions of the form 'p implies q' containing only logical constants.

I hold that a word need not stand for any entity in order to contribute to a sentence's meaning; apparent names and definite phrases can be analysed away, so numbers and classes need not be treated as timeless objects.
